answer_text:
We simplify first:

\[
x=\frac{n!\binom{m}{n}}{m^n}
\]

Since

\[
\binom{m}{n}=\frac{m!}{n!(m-n)!},
\]

we get

\[
n!\binom{m}{n}=\frac{m!}{(m-n)!}=m(m-1)\cdots(m-n+1).
\]

Therefore,

\[
x=\frac{m(m-1)\cdots(m-n+1)}{m^n}
=\prod_{k=0}^{n-1}\left(1-\frac{k}{m}\right).
\]

This is the probability that \(n\) independent draws from \(m\) possibilities are all distinct.

Now substitute the given scale:

\[
m=52!\approx 8.06\times 10^{67},
\qquad
n\approx 10^{14}.
\]

So

\[
\frac{n}{m}\approx \frac{10^{14}}{8.06\times 10^{67}}
\approx 1.24\times 10^{-54},
\]

which is extraordinarily small.

Using the standard approximation

\[
\prod_{k=0}^{n-1}\left(1-\frac{k}{m}\right)
\approx \exp\left(-\frac{n(n-1)}{2m}\right),
\]

we estimate

\[
\frac{n(n-1)}{2m}
\approx
\frac{10^{28}}{2(8.06\times 10^{67})}
\approx 6.2\times 10^{-41}.
\]

Thus

\[
x\approx \exp\left(-6.2\times 10^{-41}\right)
\approx 1-6.2\times 10^{-41}.
\]

This is indistinguishable from \(1\) for any practical purpose. It is not close to \(0\).

\[
\boxed{1}
\]
